newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Zaire civilians, soldiers flee to Tanzania.
newsitem.headline: Zaire civilians, soldiers flee to Tanzania.

text.p: Up to 1,500 civilians are crossing Lake Tanganyika daily to escape rebel advances in eastern Zaire, joined by smaller numbers of ragged Zairean soldiers, according to U.N. officials and Tanzanian authorities.
United Nations refugee officials said on Sunday there were already more than 15,000 Zairean refugees in camps around Kigoma on the eastern shore of the lake in Tanzania.

The latest group of 50 Zairean soldiers -- demoralised, ill-equipped and wearing tattered uniforms -- reached Kigoma on Friday, the semi-official Sunday News quoted acting regional commissioner Alhaj Ahmed Lugusha as saying.
"Most of them had talismans tied to their arms or waists -- rolls of bhang (marijuana) and other substances -- suggesting their reliance on sorcery in fighting the rebels," he said.
Last Thursday 161 Zairean soldiers, heavily armed with guns, grenades and ammunition, arrived in Kigoma by boat. They were disarmed and detained, Lugusha said.
The rebels, who have seized a large part of eastern Zaire since October, overran the Kalemie, the main Zairean port on Lake Tanganyika, two weeks ago.
Up to 1,500 Zaireans a day had been crossing Lake Tanganyika to seek refuge in Tanzania over the last three weeks, the U.N. officials said.
Lugusha said Tanzanian security forces in the area were on the alert for further arrivals after reports of continued fighting on the Zaire shore of the lake.
Tanzania had several hundred thousand refugees from other Central African crises living on its soil last year.

Nearly all of the more than half a million Rwandan refugees in Tanzania returned home in December after Tanzania ordered them to leave by the end of 1996. They had fled to Tanzania fearing retribution for the 1994 genocide of an estimated 800,000 minority Tutsis and allied Hutus by Hutu hardliners
An estimated 200,000 refugees from Burundi are still in Tanzania, some from as far back as 1972, officials said.
On a brief visit to Kigoma on Friday, U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata saw 600 Zairean refugees arrive in three crowded boats.

Ogata told reporters: "A continued influx of refugees on this scale will pose serious problems for the U.N. refugee officials. They had not anticipated the arrival of such numbers. But they are doing their best to cope."
Hundreds of refugees were in temporary accommodation in a sports stadium in Kigoma, before being moved to camps further away from the port.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila addressed a crowd of 1,500 people in Kalemie, 150 km (100 miles) southwest of Kigoma, on Saturday and 4,000 of his troops paraded through the town.
Food and other supplies are short in Kalemie, and a cholera outbreak in the area has killed more than 300 people in the last few weeks, arriving refugees told U.N. officials in Kigoma.
